mcqs.q: In the temporomandibular joint, the mandible articulates with the:
mcqs.explain: The TMJ is where the mandible articulates with the temporal bone of the cranium.

mcqs.q: The TMJ develops embryologically from the:
mcqs.explain: The TMJ develops (6th–8th week IUL) from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), with condylar and temporal blastemas.

mcqs.q: The articular disc of the TMJ forms (by condensation of mesenchyme) at about:
mcqs.explain: The articular disc develops around the 12th week, after the joint cavities form (10th–12th week).

mcqs.q: Full functional maturation of the TMJ is usually achieved by:
mcqs.explain: The TMJ is structurally present at birth, but full maturation/calcification is achieved by 16–20 years.

mcqs.q: The TMJ is classified as a ginglymo-arthrodial joint, meaning it allows:
mcqs.explain: Ginglymoid (hinge) gives rotation for initial opening/closing; arthrodial (gliding) gives forward/backward sliding of the condyle and disc.

mcqs.q: The hinge movement of the TMJ is responsible for:
opts: Initial opening and closing of the mouth (condyle rotation)
mcqs.explain: The hinge (ginglymoid) movement is rotation of the condyle in its socket — the initial opening and closing of the mouth.

mcqs.q: The mandibular (glenoid) fossa is described as:
opts: An oblong S-shaped cavity on the squamous temporal bone
A flat plate on the maxilla
A round socket in the mandible
mcqs.explain: The mandibular fossa is an oblong, S-shaped cavity on the undersurface of the squamous portion of the temporal bone.

mcqs.q: The articular eminence is:
opts: The transverse bony bar forming the anterior root of the zygoma
mcqs.explain: The articular eminence is the transverse bony bar (anterior root of the zygomatic arch), anterior to the mandibular fossa.

mcqs.q: The articular surface of the mandibular condyle is covered by:
mcqs.explain: Unlike most synovial joints, the TMJ condyle is covered by fibrocartilage; the condyle has medial and lateral poles.

mcqs.q: The TMJ articular disc is:
mcqs.explain: The disc is fibrous connective tissue, devoid of blood vessels or nerves (only its extreme periphery is slightly innervated).

mcqs.q: In a normal joint, the condyle sits on which part of the disc?
mcqs.explain: The disc has anterior, intermediate and posterior bands; normally the condyle articulates on the intermediate zone.

mcqs.q: The articular disc divides the joint into:
opts: Upper and lower compartments that normally do not communicate
mcqs.explain: The disc and its attachments divide the joint into upper and lower compartments that normally do not communicate.

mcqs.q: The roof of the UPPER joint compartment is the:
mcqs.explain: Upper compartment: roof = mandibular fossa, floor = superior disc surface. Lower: roof = inferior disc, floor = condyle.

mcqs.q: The PRIMARY mechanism of TMJ lubrication is:
mcqs.explain: Boundary lubrication is the primary mechanism preventing friction in the moving joint; weeping lubrication operates under compressive forces.

mcqs.q: How many FUNCTIONAL ligaments support the TMJ?
mcqs.explain: Three functional ligaments (collateral, capsular, temporomandibular) plus two accessory ligaments (sphenomandibular, stylomandibular).

mcqs.q: The collateral (discal) ligament functions to:
opts: Restrict movement of the disc away from the condyle
mcqs.explain: The collateral (discal) ligaments restrict movement of the disc away from the condyle.

mcqs.q: The temporomandibular ligament limits:
opts: Excessive dropping and posterior movement of the condyle/disc
mcqs.explain: The temporomandibular ligament resists excessive dropping of the condyle and limits its posterior movement.

mcqs.q: The accessory ligament that limits excessive PROTRUSION of the mandible is the:
mcqs.explain: The stylomandibular ligament limits excessive protrusive movement; the sphenomandibular ligament has little limiting effect.

mcqs.q: Which are the PRIMARY muscles of mastication?
opts: Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid
mcqs.explain: The primary muscles are masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid; the suprahyoid group are secondary.

mcqs.q: The blood supply of the TMJ comes from the:
mcqs.explain: Branches of the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries supply the TMJ; the veins follow the arteries.

mcqs.q: The main nerve supply of the TMJ is the:
mcqs.explain: The auriculotemporal nerve (with deep temporal and masseteric nerves) supplies the TMJ.

mcqs.q: Which imaging modality is best for the soft tissues (the disc) of the TMJ?
mcqs.explain: MRI images the soft tissues — joint effusion (T2-weighted) and disc displacement (T1-weighted); panoramic/CBCT show the bone.

mcqs.q: On the histological section, the TMJ joint space appears on radiographs as a:
mcqs.explain: On conventional radiographs and CT, the joint space appears as a radiolucent space between the condyle and fossa.

mcqs.q: The condylar cartilage of the developing TMJ is important because it:
opts: Serves as a growth site for the mandible
mcqs.explain: The condylar cartilage acts as a growth site; the TMJ continues remodeling postnatally with eruption and mastication.

saqs.q: Outline the embryological development of the TMJ.
saqs.a: From the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage): 6–8 wk condylar/temporal blastemas; 10–12 wk mesenchyme splits into upper & lower cavities; ~12 wk the articular disc condenses; matures by 16–20 y.

saqs.q: Describe the joint type and movements of the TMJ.
saqs.a: A synovial ginglymo-arthrodial joint: hinge (rotation) for initial opening/closing, and gliding (translation) — forward/backward sliding of the condyle and disc.

saqs.q: List the bony components of the TMJ.
saqs.a: Mandibular (glenoid) fossa (S-shaped, squamous temporal), articular eminence (anterior root of zygoma), and the mandibular condyle (medial/lateral poles, fibrocartilage-covered).

saqs.q: Describe the articular disc and the joint compartments.
saqs.a: Fibrous, avascular, non-innervated disc (anterior/intermediate/posterior bands); condyle rests on the intermediate zone. It divides the joint into upper & lower compartments that don't communicate.

saqs.q: Name the ligaments of the TMJ.
saqs.a: Functional: collateral (discal), capsular, temporomandibular. Accessory: sphenomandibular and stylomandibular (limits protrusion).

saqs.q: State the muscles, blood and nerve supply of the TMJ.
saqs.a: Muscles: masseter, temporalis, medial & lateral pterygoid. Blood: superficial temporal & maxillary arteries. Nerve: auriculotemporal (+ deep temporal/masseteric).

saqs.q: Which imaging modalities are used for the TMJ?
saqs.a: Panoramic/CBCT for the osseous structures; MRI for the soft tissues/disc (effusion on T2, disc displacement on T1); ultrasonography.
